newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu returns to his frightened capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu returns to his frightened capital.

text.p: Zaire's veteran president, Mobutu Sese Seko, returned to his frightened capital on Thursday after efforts to stage last-ditch peace talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila collapsed.

State television showed Mobutu, who is fighting cancer and a seven-month-old civil war, descending the steps of his plane on the arm of his wife Bobi Ladawa after flying in from the port of Pointe Noire in neighbouring Congo, where he spent the night.
"Bloodbath" was a word on many lips in Kinshasa as the teeming capital of five million people prepared for the worst.
"We're heading directly for a bloodbath. It's a question of balance of forces. Kabila knows he has the upper hand," said Mobutu aide Kabuya Lumuna.
"Confrontation is inevitable. We will have two or three bad days from now on," Mobutu opponent Mukendi wa Mulumba said.
Britain urged its nationals to leave Kinshasa in a message broadcast over the BBC World Service.

"The situation is increasingly volatile in the Kinshasa area," the Foreign Office said. "There can be no guarantee of safety for the British community or registered Commonwealth nationals who choose to remain."
Mobutu's flight may prove the last into the city. An airline office in a downtown hotel said that the airport, which is 25 km (16 miles) from the centre of the city, was effectively closed.
Witnesses said the road to the airport was eery and largely deserted, apart from security forces. The last commercial flight, South African Airways, left on Wednesday.
Officals in Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo, said ferry services across the river from Kinshasa had halted. One official said Zairean customs officers had shut their offices.
South Africa's Nelson Mandela, who has been trying to avert a battle for Kinshasa, cancelled Wednesday's planned shipboard summit after Kabila, citing security concerns, failed to show.
But despite the misgivings in Kinshasa, where residents fear a rampage by Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined army as much as anything else, mediation efforts continued.
Kabila, whose forces control three-quarters of Africa's third largest nation, arrived in Cape Town for talks with Mandela on Thursday.
"Our negotiations have not finished because we are still waiting for Mr Mobutu's reply," Kabila's foreign affairs spokesman Bizima Karaha told Radio France International.
Mobutu's emergency-rule government took a similar line. "We do not think that the dialogue has broken down," spokesman Kin-Kiey Mulumba said on Wednesday.
But rebel justice "commissioner-general" Mwenze Kongolo, quoted by Portugal's news agency Lusa from Cabinda, said Mobutu ran the risk of capture if he remained in power until Saturday.
Kabila declined to join Mandela and Mobutu on a South African ship moored in Pointe Noire, demanding that the talks take place in international waters.
Mobutu has dominated what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries since seizing power in 1965.

He agreed at peace talks on May 4 to hand power to an elected president. Kabila, then and in public statements since, has insisted Mobutu hand power at once to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
"They want the head of state to leave but we cannot agree how to do it," Kabuya, the Mobutu aide, told Reuters.
The government maintains that rebel forces are being held up by the army some 200 km (120 miles) east of Kinshasa. The rebels say they are much closer to the city.
The opposition newspaper La Reference Plus feared the worst. "Big dictators only negotiate their departure on the basis of a bloodbath," it said in an editorial.

Across the river in Brazzaville, capital of Congo, U.S., British, French, Belgian and Portuguese troops were waiting with helicopters and fast boats to pluck foreign nationals to safety should Kinshasa become a battleground.
